concept: Atlas Query Profiler and Operation Throttling metrics
summary: Source-anchored research for Atlas Query Profiler and Operation Throttling metrics. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: In a firsthand forum report, the author initially saw long Datadog MongoDB spans missing from Atlas profiling and later attributed the load-test bottleneck to the Heroku application server, reporting that the queries were absent from MongoDB logs. This is one anecdote supporting investigation of application-side delay, not proof of a general profiler defect or a universal root cause. (low confidence)

MongoDB's Atlas resilience workflow uses Query Profiler to identify an expensive query shape, then monitors Operation Throttling in cluster Metrics after query rejection or timeout. Use both views when assessing containment; they answer different diagnostic questions. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Atlas manages the slow-operation threshold dynamically; MongoDB documents this per mongod host based on average operation execution time. AWS independently documents disabling the managed threshold before collecting comprehensive Atlas logs for its compatibility tool. Therefore, do not assume every Atlas workload uses a fixed 100 ms logging threshold. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Query Profiler is a sampled, batched view: the documented display limit is 100,000 data points, data may lag by up to five minutes, and activity spikes can suspend UI log collection. Zooming can change sampling fidelity. MongoDB directs users to downloaded mongod logs for exact unsampled counts of logged operations; this does not imply every database operation was logged. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

The Atlas resilience guide describes copying queryShapeHash from a slow-query detail panel and using setQuerySettings to reject that query shape. It directs operators to the selected shard under Metrics > MongoDB Metrics > Operation Throttling to monitor after rejection or timeout. This is a mitigation workflow, not automatic index repair. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Percona's firsthand diagnostic examples include an Atlas network-retransmission incident in which the server answered quickly, and a laboratory inefficient-query incident without a useful log entry. Application latency alone therefore cannot identify expensive sort execution; correlate query evidence with host metrics. (low confidence)

Atlas Query Profiler identifies inefficient operations from mongod log entries. It differs from the Database Profiler, which records operations according to its profiling level; changing that level alone does not change the slow queries displayed in Atlas Query Profiler. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

The Atlas Query Profiler documentation limits the tool to M10+ clusters. Its selectable metrics include execution time, documents examined and returned, keys examined, yields, response size, and examined-to-returned ratios; query details expose the query shape, execution statistics and log entry. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Methodological inference for SORT_MERGE investigations: use Query Profiler to locate the expensive operation, then inspect the actual explain stage tree. The profiler hasSort and usedIndex flags describe broad operation properties and do not by themselves establish a particular execution stage. Explain documents the winning plan as named stages with child stages. (medium confidence)

The Atlas Query Profiler documentation excludes bulk writes from its sampling and analysis, including bulkWrite and updateMany operations with multiple stmtIds. Absence from this view is consequently insufficient evidence that such operations did not occur. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

MongoDB Ops Manager explicitly defines its Operation Throttling series: rejected counts operations matching user-defined rejection filters, while killed counts read operations exceeding the default cluster timeout. The retrieved Atlas resilience guide associates its same-named chart with rejection and timeout, but its extracted text omits the series definitions; the exact Atlas series mapping therefore remains unconfirmed by the readable Atlas text. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

The Atlas resilience guide introduces cluster-level read timeout protection with defaultMaxTimeMS in MongoDB 8.0; an operation-level maxTimeMS can override that default. The Ops Manager metric documentation likewise says operation-level timeouts override the cluster-level timeout. These are execution timeout controls, not a setting that selects a sort plan. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Atlas documents Operation Rate Limiting separately from Operation Throttling. Its rate-limiter metrics include offered, successful and rejected operation rates, queue time and queue depth. Datadog separately exposes mongodb.atlas.network.ingressRequestRateLimiter.rejectedAdmissions and averageTimeQueuedMicros; these names refer to ingress admission, so they should not be silently substituted for query-shape rejection or default-timeout counters. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Datadog exposes mongodb.atlas.metrics.queryexecutor.scannedperreturned and mongodb.atlas.metrics.queryexecutor.scannedobjectsperreturned as targeting-efficiency gauges. Atlas Query Profiler offers keys-examined-to-returned and documents-examined-to-returned ratios for individual logged operations. These provide complementary efficiency signals, not a dedicated SORT_MERGE counter. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Profiler omissions do not establish absence of expensive work: bulk writes are excluded, and high log volume can suspend UI log collection. MongoDB states that downloadable logs remain complete despite UI analysis rate limits. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

MongoDB 8.0 introduced operation rejection filters for blocking new executions of an identified query shape. The documented Atlas workflow copies queryShapeHash from profiler details and supplies it to setQuerySettings; operation rejection requires the atlasAdmin role. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Datadog documents mongodb.atlas.global.lock.current.queue.reads, .writes, and .total as gauges of operations waiting for locks. These describe lock queues; they should not be substituted for the Atlas Operation Throttling chart without a verified mapping. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

A practical investigation should align host and time across profiler evidence and system metrics before attributing latency to a query. MongoDB provides host/time profiler filters, while Percona demonstrates network and storage incidents that require metrics beyond query logs. (medium confidence)
